text: Greedy rules, the proofs that justify them, and the counterexamples that break them.

A greedy algorithm builds the answer one step at a time, always taking the choice that looks best right now, and never undoing it. It is short and fast, but only correct when you can prove that a locally best choice never spoils the overall best answer.

Two standard proofs. Exchange argument: take any optimal answer that differs from the greedy one, swap one piece to match greedy, and show it gets no worse. Stays ahead: after every step, greedy is at least as good as any other method so far.
greedy 3, best 2
greedy 2, best 2
With coins 4, 3, 1, greedy pays 6 as 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins), but 3 + 3 needs only two. "Take the biggest coin" is correct for some coin systems (1, 2, 5, 10 …) and wrong for others.
Before trusting a greedy rule, compare it with a slow brute force on many small random inputs (a stress test). One mismatch kills the rule; no mismatches is evidence, and then look for the proof.

title: Sort by a ratio: partial knapsack

text: Gold dust can be split, so value per unit weight is all that matters: take the richest pile first, then the next, and cut the last one to fit (P2240).
Compare ratios v₁/w₁ > v₂/w₂ as v1 * w2 > v2 * w1 : exact in integers. When items cannot be split (0/1 knapsack), this greedy is wrong; that needs dynamic programming.
order a b : a waits 0, b waits t_a order b a : b waits 0, a waits t_b everyone behind waits t_a + t_b either way, so put the shorter one first: t_a < t_b

Swapping two neighbours changes only their own waits, so any order with a longer job before a shorter one can be improved by a swap. Hence sorted by time is optimal (P1223). pair sorts by the first field, then the second; t[i].first and t[i].second read the two fields.
[0,2) [1,3) [2,4) [3,6) pick the earliest finish that does not overlap

Taking the contest that ends first leaves the most time for the rest; any optimal plan can swap its first contest for this one without losing anything (P1803). Sorting by start time or by length both fail on small examples.

title: More greedy rules from this list

text: Smallest number after deleting k digits: whenever a digit is larger than the one after it, deleting it helps most, because it sits in a higher place (P1106). Filling pits: a day of work covers one continuous stretch, so only each rise from the previous depth costs extra days (P5019).

Pairing: the most expensive souvenir must leave; let it take the cheapest one with it if they fit; two pointers after sorting (P1094). Adjacent sums: when a pair is too large, eating from the right box also lowers the next pair, so it is never worse (P3817).

Biggest number from concatenation: sort with a + b > b + a (P1012). The king's game sorts ministers by a × b and needs big numbers (P1080). Picking cheapest first (P1208, P1478) and alternating tallest and shortest jumps (P4995) are sort-then-scan greedies; prove each with an exchange of two neighbours.
Always merge the two smallest: priority queues and optimal codes.
14 = a 5 + b 9 (one level lower)

Huffman coding gives frequent characters short codes and rare ones long codes. Build a tree: repeatedly take the two smallest weights, join them under a new node whose weight is their sum, and put it back. Each character's code length is its depth.
The total cost (sum of frequency × code length) equals the sum of all the joined weights. Why greedy works: the two rarest symbols can always be placed deepest, as siblings, in some optimal tree.

priority_queue keeps the largest element on top; with greater<long long> it keeps the smallest. push and pop cost O(log n), so n merges cost O(n log n) (P1090: merging fruit heaps is exactly a Huffman tree).
Sorting once is not enough: each merged heap must go back among the others, possibly in the middle. That is why a priority queue is used.
total bits 224

Store the tree as a parent array: leaves are 0 … n − 1, each merge creates the next node number. Following parents up from a leaf gives its depth, which is its code length. Check: 5·4 + 9·4 + 12·3 + 13·3 + 16·3 + 45·1 = 224.
